::: {.callout-warning title="Conditions of Use"} - This document is intended for personal use and is NOT meant to be shared on the internet (e.g. Studocu, ThinkSwap, StudentVIP, Coursehero, etc.) - Do not share this document with anyone, even if they are enrolled in ECOM30004/90004. - Official course materials, such as lecture slides, tutorial sheets and prescribed readings should always be your primary point of reference. ::: ## A little about me... - Pengyun (Kevin) Chen - I am a third-year PhD student in Economics. - My research interests are financial econometrics, empirical macro, and more recently, energy economics and sustainable finance. ::: {.callout-tip title="Help me help you"} Please let me know if: - you have got questions to ask and/or I have made some mistakes - you want me to repeat something - you have general feedback/suggestions on improvements I really value and appreciate that! ::: - Get in touch: `kevin.chen10@unimelb.edu.au` ## Tutorial Preparation and Expectations ::: {.my-list} - Tutorials start in Week 1. I take two tutorials each week:
| Day/Time | Location | Tutorial Code | |:------------------:|:--------------:|:--------------:| | Wednesday 1:00pm | The Spot-3014 | T01/06 | | Wednesday 2:00pm | The Spot-3014 | T01/05 |
- The software used for ECOM30004/90004 are **R and RStudio**, so these should be installed onto your computer as you will need them for completing tutorial tasks and assignments. - From Week 2 the tutorial will build on the lecture and self-directed activities from the previous week. You are expected to have attended or viewed the lecture and carried out the self-directed activities. - There will be a weekly homework submission following each tutorial, starting from Week 2. (more on next slide) ::: ## Tutorial Attendance and Homework (10% Assessment) - You should attend the tutorial you are officially enrolled in. - You must contact me in advance (e.g. by email) if you need to attend one of my other tutorial sessions. - Approval is subject to available capacity and obtained on a weekly basis. - **Starting from Week 3**, each week there will be 1 mark allocated if you *both* - attend the tutorial, *and* - by 11am Monday submit solutions to the previous week's self-directed activities on the LMS. - **Example:** the second self-directed activities will be first to be submitted, by Monday 11am of Week 3. ## This tutorial - This tutorial will revise/introduce some relevant R commands for this subject. - Introduce data on Retail sales for Australia that will be used for the first forecasting application in this subject. - Retail sales are considered a key indicator of the health of an economy, and are commonly a target of interest for commercial forecasters. Before starting with the questions, let's warm up by setting up our workspace in RStudio. Usually the first step is to set up the **working directory**. --- ### Warming Up: Setting Up Working Directory in R ::: {.callout-note} Setting up the working directory ensures that R can accurately locate where your data files are stored. It defines where R looks for files and where it saves outputs. ::: To set up your working directory, enter command: ```{r} #| echo: true #| eval: false setwd("Your location goes here") ```
Alternatively, you can click on: $$\boxed{\;\textsf{Session}\;}\;\;\to\;\;\boxed{\;\textsf{Set Working Directory}\;}\;\;\to\;\;\boxed{\;\textsf{Choose Directory}\;}$$ On my computer, it looks like: --- ### Warming Up: Checking Working Directory in R To check your working directory, enter `getwd()` into your Console tab: ```{r} #| echo: true #| eval: true getwd() ```
Your working directory is also displayed here (above the Console window):
:::{.callout-tip} If the folder looks correct, you can proceed to loading the datasets and files. ::: ## Warming Up: Some Useful Functions - To execute a single line of code: - To clear Console window: $$\begin{aligned} \textsf{Windows:}&\;\;\boxed{\;\textsf{Ctrl}\;} + \boxed{\;\textsf{L}\;}\\ \textsf{Mac:}&\;\;\boxed{\;\textsf{control}\;} + \boxed{\;\textsf{L}\;}\quad\quad\textsf{(Note: not $\boxed{\;\textsf{Command}\;}$)}\\ \end{aligned}$$ - To recall the previous command(s) you have entered, press $\boxed{\;\uparrow\;}$ in Console. - To obtain help: ```{r} #| echo: true #| eval: false help(aggregate) ?aggregate # Same as help() function ??aggregate # If you want to know which package it is from ``` ## Question 1 ::: {.callout-question} Obtain the data file `RetailSales.csv`, and save it into an appropriate working directory. Read the data into an R dataframe. To get a sense of the variables in the dataframe, use the `head()` command to print out the first six rows of the dataframe. :::
```{r} #| echo: true #| eval: true # Read data file and create monthly ts object dt <- read.csv("RetailSales.csv") print(head(dt)) ``` ## Question 2 ::: {.callout-question} We will focus on the time series of Total retail sales. Create a time series object for monthly total retail sales. Plot this time series. :::
```{r} #| echo: true #| eval: true Retail_m <- ts(dt$Total, frequency=12, start=c(1982,4), end=c(2024,9)) plot(Retail_m, main="Monthly Australian Retail Sales", ylab="Retail sales ($m)") ``` ## Question 3(a) {.scrollable .shrink-output} ::: {.callout-question} Use `aggregate` to transform the monthly time series to quarterly frequency. :::
```{r} #| echo: true #| eval: true Retail_q <- aggregate(Retail_m, nfrequency=4) ```
❓ What's going on? ::: {.small-output} ```{r} #| echo: true #| eval: true print(Retail_m) ```
```{r} #| echo: true #| eval: true print(Retail_q) ``` :::
::: {.callout-note} `aggregate` generates a new series, `Retail_q`, by summing up the monthly observations of each quarter. ::: ## Question 3(b) ::: {.callout-question} Create a window of this quarterly time series from 2000q1 to 2018q4, and produce a time series plot. :::
```{r} #| echo: true #| eval: true S_t <- window(Retail_q, start=c(2000,1), end=c(2018,4)) plot(S_t, main="Quarterly Australian Retail Sales", ylab="Retail sales ($m)") ``` ## Question 4 ::: {.callout-question} Take the log of the quarterly time series and produce a plot. :::
```{r} Y_t <- log(S_t) plot(Y_t, main="Retail sales (log), 2000q1 to 2018q4") ``` ## Questions 5 and 6 ::: {.callout-question} Denote the log retail sales time series as $Y_{t}$. Create the *first difference* time series $$\Delta Y_{t}=Y_{t}-Y_{t-1}$$ Print out the first six values of $Y_{t}$ and $\Delta Y_{t}$. What’s going on with the value of $\Delta Y_{t}$ for 2000q1? :::
```{r} # First difference of quarterly log retail sales Y_t, convert to pct D_Y_t <- diff(Y_t)*100 print(round(head(cbind(Y_t,D_Y_t)),4)) ```
::: {.callout-note} The first value in `D_Y_t` is missing (`NA`) because there is no value of `Y_t` available before 10.3685 to compute the difference. Taking a difference of a time series will necessarily result in a shorter time series because of this. ::: ## Question 7 ::: {.callout-question} Denote the quarterly retail sales time series by $S_{t}$. Create a time series of the quarterly percentage change (growth rate) of this time series, that is $$R_{t}=\frac{S_{t}-S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}}\times 100\%.$$ Compare the values of $\Delta Y_{t}$ and $R_{t}$. :::
```{r} # Percentage change of retail sales R_t <- diff(S_t)/lag(S_t,-1)*100 # Compare print(round(head(cbind(D_Y_t, R_t)),4)) ``` ## Question 7 ::: {.callout-question} Denote the quarterly retail sales time series by $S_{t}$. Create a time series of the quarterly percentage change (growth rate) of this time series, that is $$R_{t}=\frac{S_{t}-S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}}\times 100\%.$$ Compare the values of $\Delta Y_{t}$ and $R_{t}$. :::
What does `lag(S_t, -1)` function do? ```{r} print(head(cbind(lag(S_t,-1),S_t))) ``` ## Question 7 ctd: Why the comparison? :::{.incremental} - Adding 1 on both sides and take logs: \begin{align} R_{t}&=\frac{S_{t}-S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}}\\ 1+R_{t}&=\frac{S_{t}}{S_{t-1}}\\ \log(1+R_{t})&=\log(S_{t})-\log(S_{t-1})\\ \log(1+R_{t})&=Y_{t}-Y_{t-1}\equiv\Delta Y_{t} \end{align} - Then with the approximation $\log(1+R_{t})\approx R_{t}$ for small values of $R_{t}$, we have $R_{t}\approx \Delta Y_{t}$: $$\text{$R_{t}\approx\log(1+R_{t})$}= \Delta Y_{t}$$ ::: ## Question 7 continued Why is $\ln(1+x)\approx x$ for small values of $x$?
## Question 7 ctd: Some further observations (1/2) ::: {.callout-question} Denote the quarterly retail sales time series by $S_{t}$. Create a time series of the quarterly percentage change (growth rate) of this time series, $R_{t}=\frac{S_{t}-S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}}\times 100\%$. Compare the values of $\Delta Y_{t}$ and $R_{t}$. :::
::: {.callout-note} The values of $\log S_{t}-\log S_{t-1}$ and $R_{t}=(S_{t}-S_{t-1})/S_{t-1}$ are quite similar especially for the smaller changes. :::
For the entire time series the two variables are very highly correlated: ```{r} print(cor(R_t, D_Y_t)) print(round(cor(R_t, D_Y_t), 3)) ``` ## Question 7 ctd: Some further observations (2/2) ::: {.callout-note} The values of $\log S_{t}-\log S_{t-1}$ and $R_{t}=(S_{t}-S_{t-1})/S_{t-1}$ are quite similar especially for the smaller changes. :::
This is also evident in the plot shown below: ```{r} plot(as.numeric(R_t), as.numeric(D_Y_t), pch=16, cex=0.7, xlab="Rt", ylab="DYt") lines(as.numeric(R_t), as.numeric(R_t), col="blue") ``` ## Question 7 ctd: Why taking logs differences? - Taking log differences or simple returns is a common type of "filtering" in time series analysis. - Filtering tends to stablise/linearise features such as trend and seasonality. - Changes in a logged time series can be interpreted as approximately percentage changes, which is often convenient. - Also, time series models, such as AR models and VAR models, requires data to be *stationary* $\to$ filtering/transformation ensures this requirement is met. ## {data-background-color="#000F46"}
Thank you for coming!
